## Where it started

## Decisions locked + what shipped

- `lsat-session-lesson` is the single active post-session skill. It owns transcript intake, the primary student record, lecture-style teaching, the interactive preview, verification, and filing.
- The former `session-recap` procedure is now an internal reference. Its active copies were retired and preserved under `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os\skills\_retired\session-recap-2026-09-30\`.
- Natural triggers include “Curray session,” “[student] session,” “make a recap,” “session notes,” and “write up this transcript.” A request only to find or inspect a transcript stays narrow.
- The unified skill was synced across Codex, Claude, and Gemini, committed as `4b1f49d`, and pushed to `main`. No student lesson was created or assigned in this consolidation.

## Key files for next session

- `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os\.agents\skills\lsat-session-lesson\references\transcript-intake-and-record.md` — Calendar and Drive intake, recap format, and filing rules.
- `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os\.agents\skills\lsat-session-lesson\references\lesson-quality-bar.md` — teaching and interactive-note acceptance criteria.

## Running state

- Background processes: none.
- Dev servers / ports: none started for this work.
- Open worktrees / branches: no worktree created; AI OS is on `main`.

## Verification — how to confirm things still work

- `git status --short` in `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — working tree was clean after the push.
- `rg -n "lsat-session-lesson|session-recap" skills/INDEX.md` — the generated index lists the unified skill and no active `session-recap` entry.
- `py system/scripts/check-skills.py` — still fails on three unrelated existing issues: a stale `gws-gmail` activation copy and two root-instruction path checks. Targeted consolidation checks passed.

## Deferred + open questions

- Deferred: the three broader skill-validator issues; they were outside this consolidation.
- Open: none.

## Pick up here

For the next post-session request, activate `lsat-session-lesson` directly and follow its intake reference through the finished student note.

# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus
consultations. Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.

- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Routing map

Paths are relative to the repository root.

Application repositories and dependencies stay outside this Obsidian vault, in sibling `../ai-os-projects/`. Do not create a junction from the vault back into that directory.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex and Claude both activate the LLM Wiki ingest, query, and lint workflows. Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

</INSTRUCTIONS>

The earlier versions below are preserved history. The marked V3 block is the current export source.\\r\\n  16: \\r\\n  17: # Conditional Must Be True: Keep the Whole Statement\\r\\n  18: \\r\\n  19: Only people willing to compromise should undergo mediation. This tells you what is required for mediation to be appropriate. It does not tell you who actually attends, or whether willingness alone is enough. Keeping those distinctions intact is the work of conditional reasoning.\\r\\n  20: \\r\\n  21: ## Combine what the statements guarantee\\r\\n  22: \\r\\n  23: A Must Be True answer must follow from the information you were given. Sometimes you combine facts. Sometimes you connect rules. Identify what each sentence gives you before choosing a method.\\r\\n  24: \\r\\n  25: Suppose one type of flavonoid found in apples is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. You can conclude that at least one type of flavonoid found in apples helps prevent heart disease.\\r\\n  26: \\r\\n  27: Why at least one? The first statement identifies one type with the relevant property. The second tells you what that property does. Together they support a claim about that type. They do not show that every flavonoid has the property, or that eating any apple prevents heart disease.\\r\\n  28: \\r\\n  29: Keep the strength of the conclusion equal to the strength of the evidence. Helps prevent does not mean always prevents.\\r\\n  30: \\r\\n  31: A rule works differently. If a person should undergo mediation, that person is willing to compromise tells you a relationship. It does not tell you that anyone actually should undergo mediation. A rule does not establish its own starting condition.\\r\\n  32: \\r\\n  33: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n  34: \\r\\n  35: An apple flavonoid is an antioxidant, and antioxidants help prevent heart disease. Can you conclude that every apple flavonoid prevents heart disease? Explain.\\r\\n  36: \\r\\n  37: **Worked answer:** No. The evidence establishes the relevant property for at least one type, not every type. It says helps prevent, not always prevents. A second type without that property would fit the evidence and defeat the stronger answer.\\r\\n  38: \\r\\n  39: ## Put the requirement on the right\\r\\n  40: \\r\\n  41: Consider this hypothetical rule: Only people willing to compromise should undergo mediation to resolve their conflict.\\r\\n  42: \\r\\n  43: Mediation means trying to resolve a dispute with help from a neutral person. The rule limits who should use it. Willingness to compromise is required.\\r\\n  44: \\r\\n  45: First flatten the sentence into complete English:\\r\\n  46: \\r\\n  47: If a person should undergo mediation, then that person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n  48: \\r\\n  49: Now abbreviate the complete ideas:\\r\\n  50: \\r\\n  51: M = the person should undergo mediation.\\r\\n  52: \\r\\n  53: W = the person is willing to compromise.\\r\\n  54: \\r\\n  55: M → W\\r\\n  56: \\r\\n  57: The left side is sufficient: knowing M lets you conclude W. The right side is necessary: M cannot be true without W. Necessary does not mean enough by itself. A person can meet a requirement without qualifying for the activity.\\r\\n  58: \\r\\n  59: Only if works the same way. Litigation should be pursued only if a person is sure their position is correct becomes: If the person should pursue litigation, then the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n  60: \\r\\n  61: L = the person should pursue litigation. C = the person is sure their position is correct.\\r\\n  62: \\r\\n  63: L → C\\r\\n  64: \\r\\n  65: Being sure is required. It does not establish that the person should litigate. Also, being sure that a position is correct is not the same as the position actually being correct.\\r\\n  66: \\r\\n  67: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n  68: \\r\\n  69: Only trained volunteers should lead the workshop. Write the complete if-then rule. Does training alone prove that a volunteer should lead?\\r\\n  70: \\r\\n  71: **Worked answer:** If a volunteer should lead the workshop, then that volunteer is trained. Training is required, but training alone does not prove the person should lead. Other considerations may matter. Reversing the rule would add a guarantee we were never given.\\r\\n  72: \\r\\n  73: ## Keep should in the statement\\r\\n  74: \\r\\n  75: A recommendation and an action are different ideas. A person may do something they should not do. A person may also fail to do something they should do.\\r\\n  76: \\r\\n  77: M → W is about who should undergo mediation. It is not a rule about everyone who actually undergoes mediation.\\r\\n  78: \\r\\n  79: Suppose Alex actually attends mediation but refuses to compromise. That does not contradict this rule. Alex may be doing something Alex should not do. But if we say Alex should undergo mediation and Alex is unwilling to compromise, those two claims violate the rule.\\r\\n  80: \\r\\n  81: Keep words such as should, can, must, and actually when you translate. Removing one can change what the statement proves. An abbreviation saves writing only when you remember the whole idea behind it.\\r\\n  82: \\r\\n  83: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n  84: \\r\\n  85: We know only that Morgan actually underwent mediation. Does the rule prove that Morgan was willing to compromise? Why?\\r\\n  86: \\r\\n  87: **Worked answer:** No. The rule starts with should undergo mediation, not actually underwent mediation. Morgan could have attended despite being unwilling. The actual action does not activate this recommendation rule.\\r\\n  88: \\r\\n  89: ## Reverse and negate to get the contrapositive\\r\\n  90: \\r\\n  91: The rule M → W forbids one combination: M true with W false. If willingness is absent, the recommendation cannot be present.\\r\\n  92: \\r\\n  93: M → W\\r\\n  94: \\r\\n  95: not W → not M\\r\\n  96: \\r\\n  97: In English: If a person is unwilling to compromise, then that person should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n  98: \\r\\n  99: You reverse the order and negate both complete ideas. The new statement describes the same restriction as the original. This is why it is valid.\\r\\n 100: \\r\\n 101: Reversing without negating does something different: W → M. It says willingness guarantees that mediation is appropriate. The original rule never promised that. A willing person might have a conflict for which mediation is inappropriate for another reason.\\r\\n 102: \\r\\n 103: Negating without reversing is also invalid: not M → not W. A person who should not undergo mediation could still be willing to compromise.\\r\\n 104: \\r\\n 105: The rule lets you move forward from M, or backward from not W. W alone and not M alone leave the other side open.\\r\\n 106: \\r\\n 107: ### Test every possible combination\\r\\n 108: \\r\\n 109: | Should undergo mediation | Willing to compromise | Fits M → W? |\\r\\n 110: |---|---|---|\\r\\n 111: | True | True | Yes |\\r\\n 112: | True | False | No |\\r\\n 113: | False | True | Yes |\\r\\n 114: | False | False | Yes |\\r\\n 115: \\r\\n 116: Only M true with W false violates the rule. Both states with M false are allowed. Both states with W true are allowed.\\r\\n 117: \\r\\n 118: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 119: \\r\\n 120: A volunteer is not trained. What follows from the workshop rule? What if the volunteer is trained instead?\\r\\n 121: \\r\\n 122: **Worked answer:** The untrained volunteer should not lead the workshop. That is the contrapositive: not trained → should not lead. A trained volunteer may or may not be someone who should lead. Affirming the requirement does not establish the trigger.\\r\\n 123: \\r\\n 124: ## A statement about a whole group can be a rule\\r\\n 125: \\r\\n 126: Suppose a stimulus says: People whose conflicts are based on ideology are unwilling to compromise.\\r\\n 127: \\r\\n 128: In this hypothetical stimulus, the statement applies to every person in the specified group. It is not a claim about all people, and it is not a general claim you should import into other questions.\\r\\n 129: \\r\\n 130: I = the person’s conflict is based on ideology.\\r\\n 131: \\r\\n 132: I → not W\\r\\n 133: \\r\\n 134: This is a conditional relationship even without the word if. If a person belongs to the named group, the description applies to that person. It does not establish that any particular person belongs to that group.\\r\\n 135: \\r\\n 136: Now connect it to the contrapositive:\\r\\n 137: \\r\\n 138: I → not W → not M\\r\\n 139: \\r\\n 140: Therefore: People whose conflicts are based on ideology should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n 141: \\r\\n 142: The middle idea matches exactly. The group rule gets you to unwilling to compromise. The contrapositive takes you from unwilling to compromise to should not undergo mediation.\\r\\n 143: \\r\\n 144: If the stimulus also says Lena’s conflict is based on ideology, that fact activates the chain. You can then conclude that Lena is unwilling to compromise and should not undergo mediation. Without that fact, your conclusion remains a rule about the group.\\r\\n 145: \\r\\n 146: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 147: \\r\\n 148: Use I → not W and M → W. What must follow for anyone whose conflict is based on ideology? Does that prove someone actually has such a conflict?\\r\\n 149: \\r\\n 150: **Worked answer:** I → not M. Contrapose M → W to get not W → not M, then connect I → not W → not M. The conclusion is should not undergo mediation. The group rule does not establish that a member of that group actually exists.\\r\\n 151: \\r\\n 152: ## Do not invent a choice between two activities\\r\\n 153: \\r\\n 154: The separate rule L → C gives a requirement for litigation. It does not connect litigation to mediation.\\r\\n 155: \\r\\n 156: Someone who should not undergo mediation does not automatically become someone who should pursue litigation. The stimulus has not said those are the only choices, or that every person must choose one.\\r\\n 157: \\r\\n 158: A counterexample makes the gap visible. Imagine a person who should use neither activity. That can fit both rules: the person does not have to meet the requirements for an activity they should not pursue.\\r\\n 159: \\r\\n 160: The two requirements do not create an either-or choice. You need an additional statement connecting the activities before moving from one to the other.\\r\\n 161: \\r\\n 162: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 163: \\r\\n 164: If a person should not undergo mediation, must that person pursue litigation instead? Use a counterexample.\\r\\n 165: \\r\\n 166: **Worked answer:** No. The person could appropriately pursue neither activity. That violates neither requirement. The premises do not say that mediation and litigation are exhaustive choices, or that rejecting one requires the other.\\r\\n 167: \\r\\n 168: ## Use the same process on a new question\\r\\n 169: \\r\\n 170: 1. Identify what each sentence supplies: a specific fact or a general relationship.\\r\\n 171: 2. Translate each relationship into a complete if-then sentence. Preserve the subject, negation, and words such as should.\\r\\n 172: 3. Name the complete ideas before abbreviating. Put the required condition on the right.\\r\\n 173: 4. If you need the opposite direction, reverse and negate both ideas.\\r\\n 174: 5. Connect rules only when the ending of one matches the beginning of the next. Apply a fact only when it supplies a valid starting point.\\r\\n 175: 6. Read the result back in English. Test a tempting answer by trying to make the premises true and that answer false.\\r\\n 176: \\r\\n 177: If you can build that counterexample, the answer is not guaranteed. If you cannot see a valid connection yet, do not add a fact or an extra choice to make the answer work.\\r\\n 178: \\r\\n 179: ### Put the moves together\\r\\n 180: \\r\\n 181: 1. A file may be released only if it has been reviewed. This file has not been reviewed. What follows?\\r\\n 182: \\r\\n 183: **Worked answer:** This file may not be released. May be released → reviewed; not reviewed → may not be released. Preserve permission: this does not prove that nobody actually releases it.\\r\\n 184: \\r\\n 185: 2. Only licensed drivers may operate these vans. Sam is licensed. Must Sam be permitted to operate one?\\r\\n 186: \\r\\n 187: **Worked answer:** No. May operate → licensed. Licensing is necessary, but could be insufficient. Sam could be licensed and still lack permission for another reason.\\r\\n 188: \\r\\n 189: 3. Every priority application needs supervisor approval. Approval is required only if the application is incomplete. What follows for priority applications?\\r\\n 190: \\r\\n 191: **Worked answer:** Priority → needs approval → incomplete. Every priority application is incomplete under these hypothetical rules. No particular priority application is asserted to exist.\\r\\n 192: \\r\\n 193: Transfer question: Only certified guides should lead night tours. All new guides are uncertified. Nora is a new guide. State the inference and one tempting answer that goes too far.\\r\\n 194: \\r\\n 195: **Worked answer:** New → not certified; should lead → certified; not certified → should not lead. Nora should not lead night tours. Nora never actually leads night tours goes too far: the rules concern who should lead, not what someone actually does.\\r\\n 196: \\r\\n 197: ## Before the next session\\r\\n 198: \\r\\n 199: Complete the conditional-diagramming drills first, then move into the LSAT questions. The focus is translating and diagramming conditionals until the move becomes automatic.\\r\\n 200: \\r\\n 201: ## 2026-09-30 concept extension: Choose the move the information supports\\r\\n 202: \\r\\n 203: A rule tells you what follows if a condition is met. A fact tells you what is true in a particular case. Before drawing an inference, decide which kind of information you have and where it lets you start.\\r\\n 204: \\r\\n 205: ## Apply a fact to a rule\\r\\n 206: \\r\\n 207: Suppose every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Maya submitted her application after the deadline. Maya\'s application therefore requires special approval.\\r\\n 208: \\r\\n 209: The first sentence supplies the rule. The second supplies its starting condition for one application. Together they support a conclusion about that application.\\r\\n 210: \\r\\n 211: Late application → requires special approval.\\r\\n 212: \\r\\n 213: Maya\'s application is late → Maya\'s application requires special approval.\\r\\n 214: \\r\\n 215: The fact must match the complete condition. If the rule concerns applications submitted after the deadline, knowing that an application was started after the deadline would not be enough. Started and submitted are different claims.\\r\\n 216: \\r\\n 217: This is the same issue as keeping should in the mediation statement. Actually attending mediation does not establish that someone should attend. A fact cannot activate a rule by matching only part of its wording.\\r\\n 218: \\r\\n 219: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 220: \\r\\n 221: Every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Omar\'s application requires special approval. Must Omar have submitted it after the deadline?\\r\\n 222: \\r\\n 223: **Worked answer:** No. Special approval is the result, not the starting condition. Other applications might also require it. An on-time application that needs approval for another reason fits the rule and defeats the proposed inference.\\r\\n 224: \\r\\n 225: ## Find the two starting points a rule gives you\\r\\n 226: \\r\\n 227: Use the same rule: late application → requires special approval.\\r\\n 228: \\r\\n 229: There are two facts that let you draw a definite conclusion:\\r\\n 230: \\r\\n 231: - The application is late. It requires special approval.\\r\\n 232: - The application does not require special approval. It is not late.\\r\\n 233: \\r\\n 234: The second move uses the contrapositive. A late application without the required approval condition would violate the rule, so an application lacking that condition cannot be late.\\r\\n 235: \\r\\n 236: Two other facts leave the opposite side open:\\r\\n 237: \\r\\n 238: - It requires special approval. It may or may not be late.\\r\\n 239: - It is not late. It may or may not require special approval.\\r\\n 240: \\r\\n 241: | Rule | Fact supplied | What follows |\\r\\n 242: |---|---|---|\\r\\n 243: | A → B | A | B |\\r\\n 244: | A → B | not B | not A |\\r\\n 245: | A → B | B | A remains open |\\r\\n 246: | A → B | not A | B remains open |\\r\\n 247: \\r\\n 248: Do not choose a direction merely because a sentence mentions a familiar term. Locate the fact on the rule first. A fact about the trigger or the absence of the requirement allows a move. A fact about the requirement or the absence of the trigger does not.\\r\\n 249: \\r\\n 250: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 251: \\r\\n 252: Every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Tess\'s application does not require special approval. What follows? What would follow if her application were simply not late?\\r\\n 253: \\r\\n 254: **Worked answer:** Tess\'s application is not late, by contraposition. If all we knew was that it was not late, the rule would not determine whether it required special approval. An on-time application could require approval for a different reason.\\r\\n 255: \\r\\n 256: ## Link rules before applying a fact\\r\\n 257: \\r\\n 258: Suppose every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval. Every application requiring special approval needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n 259: \\r\\n 260: Late → requires special approval → needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n 261: \\r\\n 262: Therefore, every late application needs a supervisor\'s signature. The result of the first rule supplies the starting condition of the second. That is why the chain works.\\r\\n 263: \\r\\n 264: This is still a rule. It does not establish that any application was late. If you add the fact that Maya\'s application was late, you can apply the whole chain and conclude that her application requires approval and needs a signature.\\r\\n 265: \\r\\n 266: Match the complete middle idea, including its subject and wording. Requires approval is not the same as has received approval. A rule about applications requiring approval cannot automatically connect to a rule about people granting approval.\\r\\n 267: \\r\\n 268: ### Check your reasoning\\r\\n 269: \\r\\n 270: Every urgent request needs a review. Every request needing a review requires a supervisor\'s signature. Does every urgent request require a supervisor\'s signature? Do these rules establish that an urgent request exists?\\r\\n 271: \\r\\n 272: **Worked answer:** Every urgent request requires a signature: urgent → needs review → requires signature. The rules do not establish that any urgent request exists. An additional fact would be needed to apply the rule to a particular request.\\r\\n 273: \\r\\n 274: ## Shared words do not always create a chain\\r\\n 275: \\r\\n 276: Consider two different rules:\\r\\n 277: \\r\\n 278: Late → requires special approval.\\r\\n 279: \\r\\n 280: Late → needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n 281: \\r\\n 282: Both start from late. Neither tells you that requiring approval is enough to need a signature. You cannot connect their results into requires approval → needs a signature.\\r\\n 283: \\r\\n 284: Try a counterexample: an on-time application requires special approval but does not need a supervisor\'s signature. Both rules still hold because their starting condition is absent. This defeats the proposed connection between the results.\\r\\n 285: \\r\\n 286: The same problem …6458 tokens truncated…2: <!-- TWO-MOVES -->\\r\\n  43: \\r\\n  44: **Forward:** Submitted late -> Requires approval.\\r\\n  45: \\r\\n  46: **Contrapositive:** Does not require approval -> Was not submitted late.\\r\\n  47: \\r\\n  48: The contrapositive states the same rule from its other end. Reverse the direction **and negate both complete ideas**. Simply reversing the arrow would say that requiring approval proves lateness. The original policy never said that.\\r\\n  49: \\r\\n  50: Simply negating both ideas without reversing would also add something: “not late -> does not require approval.” An on-time application could require approval for a different reason. That situation does not break the policy.\\r\\n  51: \\r\\n  52: The only combination the original rule rules out is **late, but does not require approval**. The other three combinations can fit the rule.\\r\\n  53: \\r\\n  54: <!-- CASE-GRID -->\\r\\n  55: \\r\\n  56: <!-- POP-QUIZ-1 -->\\r\\n  57: \\r\\n  58: **Try it:** Every confidential file requires restricted storage. This file does not require restricted storage. What follows? What if all you know is that it does require restricted storage?\\r\\n  59: \\r\\n  60: **Worked answer:** If it does not require restricted storage, it is not confidential. That is the contrapositive. If it does require restricted storage, its confidentiality remains unknown. A nonconfidential file could require restricted storage for another reason.\\r\\n  61: \\r\\n  62: ## 03 | Link rules when the whole middle idea matches\\r\\n  63: \\r\\n  64: Add a second policy: **Every application that requires special approval needs a supervisor\'s signature.** The first rule gets us to “requires special approval.” The second starts at that exact idea. We can carry the application through both rules.\\r\\n  65: \\r\\n  66: **First rule:** Submitted late -> Requires special approval.\\r\\n  67: \\r\\n  68: **Second rule:** Requires special approval -> Needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n  69: \\r\\n  70: **Combined rule:** Submitted late -> Needs a supervisor\'s signature.\\r\\n  71: \\r\\n  72: In letters, the pattern is `L -> R` and `R -> S`, so `L -> S`. If a particular application was late, both requirements follow for that application. Without a fact establishing a late application, we still have a combined rule rather than proof that a late application exists.\\r\\n  73: \\r\\n  74: You can also work backward through the combined rule. If an application does **not** need a supervisor\'s signature, it cannot require special approval under the second policy. If it does not require special approval, it cannot have been late under the first policy.\\r\\n  75: \\r\\n  76: **Backward chain:** Does not need signature -> Does not require approval -> Was not late.\\r\\n  77: \\r\\n  78: <!-- CHAIN-LAB -->\\r\\n  79: \\r\\n  80: ### Matching a word is not enough\\r\\n  81: \\r\\n  82: “Requires special approval” and “has received special approval” both mention approval. They describe different conditions. A requirement can exist before anyone fulfills it. You cannot link a rule ending in the first phrase to a rule starting in the second unless another statement connects them.\\r\\n  83: \\r\\n  84: This is why you should diagram **complete ideas**, not isolated words. Keep words such as “requires,” “has,” “should,” and “may” inside the condition they qualify.\\r\\n  85: \\r\\n  86: **Try it:** Every late application requires special approval. Every application that has received special approval has a supervisor\'s signature. Does a late application necessarily have a supervisor\'s signature? Explain the missing connection.\\r\\n  87: \\r\\n  88: **Worked answer:** No. A late application requires approval, but it may not have received it. The second rule applies to applications that have received approval. Nothing says the late application\'s requirement has been fulfilled.\\r\\n  89: \\r\\n  90: ## 04 | A shared starting point does not create a chain\\r\\n  91: \\r\\n  92: Compare a different pair of rules: **Every late application requires special approval. Every late application needs a supervisor\'s signature.** Both rules start at “late.” Neither starts where the other ends.\\r\\n  93: \\r\\n  94: <!-- SHARED-TRIGGER -->\\r\\n  95: \\r\\n  96: <!-- POP-QUIZ-2 -->\\r\\n  97: \\r\\n  98: If a fact tells us an application was late, we can apply **both** rules to it. That application requires approval and needs a signature. But we cannot conclude that every application requiring approval needs a signature. An on-time application might require approval for another reason without needing a signature.\\r\\n  99: \\r\\n 100: Likewise, two rules that end at the same idea do not connect their starting conditions. If confidential files require restricted storage and medical files require restricted storage, a confidential file need not be a medical file. Restricted storage could cover both types separately.\\r\\n 101: \\r\\n 102: Before joining two arrows, find the destination of the first and the starting condition of the second. They must match, including any negation or qualifier. If they do not match, keep the rules separate or see whether a valid contrapositive produces a match.\\r\\n 103: \\r\\n 104: **Try it:** Every member of a review panel has training. Every member of that panel has a security badge. Must everyone with training have a security badge? What follows if Dana is a panel member?\\r\\n 105: \\r\\n 106: **Worked answer:** Training alone does not guarantee a badge. A trained person could be outside the panel. Because Dana is a panel member, both rules apply to Dana: Dana has training and a security badge.\\r\\n 107: \\r\\n 108: ## 05 | Keep the kind of claim intact\\r\\n 109: \\r\\n 110: A rule can tell us what someone **should** do or what they **may** do. That is different from telling us what they actually did.\\r\\n 111: \\r\\n 112: Suppose **every damaged item should be inspected**. If this item is damaged, it should be inspected. We cannot conclude it has been inspected. If it is not true that an item should be inspected, it cannot be damaged under this rule. But “has not been inspected” is not the same as “it is not true that it should be inspected.” An inspection could be overdue.\\r\\n 113: \\r\\n 114: Suppose **a visitor may enter the archive only if the visitor has a badge**. A badge is necessary for permission to enter. The rule is **May enter -> Has a badge**. Without a badge, the visitor does not have permission to enter under this rule. Having a badge alone does not establish permission; another requirement might still apply.\\r\\n 115: \\r\\n 116: <!-- MODALITY -->\\r\\n 117: \\r\\n 118: The rule concerns permission. It does not prove that someone physically cannot enter without permission. Keep the same kind of claim throughout your reasoning: a requirement stays a requirement, advice stays advice, and permission stays permission.\\r\\n 119: \\r\\n 120: **Try it:** Every damaged item should be inspected. This damaged item has not been inspected. Does that violate the rule? What can you conclude about what should happen?\\r\\n 121: \\r\\n 122: **Worked answer:** The item should be inspected. Its not having been inspected does not contradict the claim about what should happen. The rule does not state that every required inspection actually occurs.\\r\\n 123: \\r\\n 124: ## 06 | Negate the whole condition\\r\\n 125: \\r\\n 126: Some conditions contain more than one part. Suppose **a document may be released only if it has been reviewed AND authorized**. Permission requires both parts. If either part is missing, the combined requirement is not satisfied.\\r\\n 127: \\r\\n 128: **Rule:** May be released -> Reviewed AND authorized.\\r\\n 129: \\r\\n 130: **Contrapositive:** Not reviewed OR not authorized -> May not be released.\\r\\n 131: \\r\\n 132: To negate “reviewed AND authorized,” you only need at least one failure. You do not need both parts to fail. “Not both” does not mean “neither.”\\r\\n 133: \\r\\n 134: Now suppose **a visitor may enter only if the visitor has a badge OR an invitation**. This requirement allows either route, including both. To fail the entire requirement, the visitor must have neither.\\r\\n 135: \\r\\n 136: **Rule:** May enter -> Has badge OR has invitation.\\r\\n 137: \\r\\n 138: **Contrapositive:** No badge AND no invitation -> May not enter.\\r\\n 139: \\r\\n 140: <!-- NEGATION -->\\r\\n 141: \\r\\n 142: Negating a compound condition changes **AND to OR**, or **OR to AND**, while negating each part. For the original AND requirement, one missing part is enough. For the original OR requirement, both routes must be missing.\\r\\n 143: \\r\\n 144: **Try it:** A document may be released only if it has been reviewed and authorized. It has been reviewed but not authorized. What follows? Does the contrapositive require us to conclude it was not reviewed?\\r\\n 145: \\r\\n 146: **Worked answer:** The document may not be released. Then choose the move the information supports.</p><div class="table-scroll"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">What you have</th><th scope="col">The move</th><th scope="col">What to check</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>A fact meeting a rule&#x27;s starting condition</td><td>Apply the rule forward</td><td>Does the whole fact match the whole condition?</td></tr><tr><td>A fact denying a rule&#x27;s required result</td><td>Use the contrapositive</td><td>Did you reverse and negate both complete ideas?</td></tr><tr><td>Two rules with a matching middle condition</td><td>Link the rules</td><td>Are direction, negation, and qualifiers identical?</td></tr><tr><td>Only the required result, or only the absence of the starting condition</td><td>Leave the other side open</td><td>Could another explanation fit the rule?</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>When an inference seems tempting, try to build a case in which the statements are true and the proposed conclusion is false. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': "   1: # Facts, Rules, and What Follows\r\n   2: \r\n   3: A rule tells you what follows **if a condition is met**. A fact tells you what is true in a particular case. Put them together, and you can prove something new.\r\n   4: \r\n   5: Suppose a program has this policy: **Every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval.** One application was submitted after the deadline. That application requires special approval. We have a rule, a fact that fits its starting condition, and a conclusion the rule guarantees.\r\n   6: \r\n   7: Change the fact, and the conclusion can change. An application that requires special approval need not have been late. It could require approval for another reason. The policy gives one route to that requirement, not the only route.\r\n   8: \r\n   9: <!-- FACT-LAB -->\r\n  10: \r\n  11: ## 01 | Start with the fact you actually have\r\n  12: \r\n  13: The rule applies to every late application. The fact identifies one of those applications. We can now apply the rule to that particular case.\r\n  14: \r\n  15: **Rule:** Every application submitted after the deadline requires special approval.\r\n  16: \r\n  17: **Fact:** This application was submitted after the deadline.\r\n  18: \r\n  19: **What follows:** This application requires special approval.\r\n  20: \r\n  21: The rule alone does not tell us that any applications were submitted late. We needed the fact to establish that we had a case to which the rule applies. A conditional rule can be true even if nothing meets its starting condition.\r\n  22: \r\n  23: Now give the two complete ideas short names. Let **L** mean “submitted after the deadline” and **R** mean “requires special approval.” The notation saves space; it should not change the meaning.\r\n  24: \r\n  25: `L -> R` means: if L is true, R must be true.\r\n  26: \r\n  27: **Try it:** Every file marked confidential requires restricted storage. This file is marked confidential. What follows? Does the rule alone establish that a confidential file exists?\r\n  28: \r\n  29: **Worked answer:** This file requires restricted storage. The fact establishes that this particular file is confidential. The rule alone establishes a requirement for any confidential file, without establishing that any such file exists.\r\n  30: \r\n  31: ## 02 | Use the rule forward, or use its contrapositive\r\n  32: \r\n  33: There are two ways to use the application policy. A late application must require approval. An application that does **not** require approval cannot have been late. If it had been late, the policy would require approval, contradicting the fact we were given.\r\n  34: \r\n  35: <!-- TWO-MOVES -->\r\n  36: \r\n  37: **Forward:** Submitted late -> Requires approval.\r\n  38: \r\n  39: **Contrapositive:** Does not require approval -> Was not submitted late.\r\n  40: \r\n  41: The contrapositive states the same rule from its other end. Reverse the direction **and negate both complete ideas**. Simply reversing the arrow would say that requiring approval proves lateness. The original policy never said that.\r\n  42: \r\n  43: Simply negating both ideas without reversing would also add something: “not late -> does not require approval.” An on-time application could require approval for a different reason. That situation does not break the policy.\r\n  44: \r\n  45: The only combination the original rule rules out is **late, but does not require approval**. The other three combinations can fit the rule.\r\n  46: \r\n  47: <!-- CASE-GRID -->\r\n  48: \r\n  49: **Try it:** Every confidential file requires restricted storage. This file does not require restricted storage. What follows? What if all you know is that it does require restricted storage?\r\n  50: \r\n  51: **Worked answer:** If it does not require restricted storage, it is not confidential. That is the contrapositive. If it does require restricted storage, its confidentiality remains unknown. A nonconfidential file could require restricted storage for another reason.\r\n  52: \r\n  53: ## 03 | Link rules when the whole middle idea matches\r\n  54: \r\n  55: Add a second policy: **Every application that requires special approval needs a supervisor's signature.** The first rule gets us to “requires special approval.” The second starts at that exact idea. We can carry the application through both rules.\r\n  56: \r\n  57: **First rule:** Submitted late -> Requires special approval.\r\n  58: \r\n  59: **Second rule:** Requires special approval -> Needs a supervisor's signature.\r\n  60: \r\n  61: **Combined rule:** Submitted late -> Needs a supervisor's signature.\r\n  62: \r\n  63: In letters, the pattern is `L -> R` and `R -> S`, so `L -> S`. If a particular application was late, both requirements follow for that application. Without a fact establishing a late application, we still have a combined rule rather than proof that a late application exists.\r\n  64: \r\n  65: You can also work backward through the combined rule. If an application does **not** need a supervisor's signature, it cannot require special approval under the second policy. If it does not require special approval, it cannot have been late under the first policy.\r\n  66: \r\n  67: **Backward chain:** Does not need signature -> Does not require approval -> Was not late.\r\n  68: \r\n  69: <!-- CHAIN-LAB -->\r\n  70: \r\n  71: ### Matching a word is not enough\r\n  72: \r\n  73: “Requires special approval” and “has received special approval” both mention approval. They describe different conditions. A requirement can exist before anyone fulfills it. You cannot link a rule ending in the first phrase to a rule starting in the second unless another statement connects them.\r\n  74: \r\n  75: This is why you should diagram **complete ideas**, not isolated words. Keep words such as “requires,” “has,” “should,” and “may” inside the condition they qualify.\r\n  76: \r\n  77: **Try it:** Every late application requires special approval. Every application that has received special approval has a supervisor's signature. Does a late application necessarily have a supervisor's signature? Explain the missing connection.\r\n  78: \r\n  79: **Worked answer:** No. A late application requires approval, but it may not have received it. The second rule applies to applications that have received approval. Nothing says the late application's requirement has been fulfilled.\r\n  80: \r\n  81: ## 04 | A shared starting point does not create a chain\r\n  82: \r\n  83: Compare a different pair of rules: **Every late application requires special approval. Every late application needs a supervisor's signature.** Both rules start at “late.” Neither starts where the other ends.\r\n  84: \r\n  85: <!-- SHARED-TRIGGER -->\r\n  86: \r\n  87: If a fact tells us an application was late, we can apply **both** rules to it. That application requires approval and needs a signature. But we cannot conclude that every application requiring approval needs a signature. An on-time application might require approval for another reason without needing a signature.\r\n  88: \r\n  89: Likewise, two rules that end at the same idea do not connect their starting conditions. If confidential files require restricted storage and medical files require restricted storage, a confidential file need not be a medical file. Restricted storage could cover both types separately.\r\n  90: \r\n  91: Before joining two arrows, find the destination of the first and the starting condition of the second. They must match, including any negation or qualifier. If they do not match, keep the rules separate or see whether a valid contrapositive produces a match.\r\n  92: \r\n  93: **Try it:** Every member of a review panel has training. Every member of that panel has a security badge. Must everyone with training have a security badge? What follows if Dana is a panel member?\r\n  94: \r\n  95: **Worked answer:** Training alone does not guarantee a badge. A trained person could be outside the panel. Because Dana is a panel member, both rules apply to Dana: Dana has training and a security badge.\r\n  96: \r\n  97: ## 05 | Keep the kind of claim intact\r\n  98: \r\n  99: A rule can tell us what someone **should** do or what they **may** do. That is different from telling us what they actually did.\r\n 100: \r\n 101: Suppose **every damaged item should be inspected**. If this item is damaged, it should be inspected. We cannot conclude it has been inspected. If an item should not be inspected, then it is not damaged under that rule. But “has not been inspected” is not the same as “should not be inspected.” An inspection could be overdue.\r\n 102: \r\n 103: Suppose **a visitor may enter the archive only if the visitor has a badge**. A badge is necessary for permission to enter. The rule is **May enter -> Has a badge**. Without a badge, the visitor does not have permission to enter under this rule. Having a badge alone does not establish permission; another requirement might still apply.\r\n 104: \r\n 105: <!-- MODALITY -->\r\n 106: \r\n 107: The rule concerns permission. It does not prove that someone physically cannot enter without permission. Keep the same kind of claim throughout your reasoning: a requirement stays a requirement, advice stays advice, and permission stays permission.\r\n 108: \r\n 109: **Try it:** Every damaged item should be inspected. This damaged item has not been inspected. Does that violate the rule? What can you conclude about what should happen?\r\n 110: \r\n 111: **Worked answer:** The item should be inspected. Its not having been inspected does not contradict the claim about what should happen. The rule does not state that every required inspection actually occurs.\r\n 112: \r\n 113: ## 06 | Negate the whole condition\r\n 114: \r\n 115: Some conditions contain more than one part. ## assistant

The main issue was the gap between a polished general lesson and a useful recap of Yahunatan’s session. His recorded difficulty was preserving the complete condition, especially **“should undergo mediation.”** The draft waits until section 5 to teach that distinction and spends its opening on a repeated late-application example.

V3 also looked like dense prose beside one widget and displayed the internal label “concept lesson.” V4 improves the presentation, adds two answerable quizzes, removes that label, and corrects a subtle negation error. It still repeats its opening example, covers substantial material beyond the session, and reveals model answers to written responses without checking their reasoning.

The canonical student recap still points to V3 and says `posted: false`; I found no evidence that V4 was assigned to the student.
